stem: A 38-year-old man with heavy daily drinking stopped 2 days ago. He is now tremulous, sweating, disoriented and hallucinating, with pulse 128/min and blood pressure 182/104 mm Hg. Serum potassium is 2.6 mEq/L. He has not vomited, has no diarrhea and takes no diuretics.
oneliner: 38M + 2 d after stopping heavy drinking + tremor, sweating, hallucinations + HR 128, BP 182/104 + K 2.6 + no vomiting, diarrhea or diuretics → why low K?
ask: Which of the following best explains his low potassium?

options.A: Catecholamines driving potassium into cells
options.B: Potassium lost in vomit
options.C: Low renin

whyNot.C: Low renin lowers aldosterone, which would **raise** potassium
whyNot.D: Muscle breakdown **releases** potassium (high K)
whyNot.E: Low urine flow **keeps** potassium in the body

answer: Catecholamine (beta-2) shift of potassium into cells
why: **Alcohol withdrawal = adrenergic storm (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating)**. Epinephrine on **beta-2 receptors switches on the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase**, moving potassium **into cells** and lowering serum K. Low magnesium in drinkers adds kidney losses.
chain: Potassium moves into cells → serum K falls

idea.rule: Things that push K into cells: insulin, beta-2 agonists (catecholamines, albuterol), alkalosis.
also: Albuterol and insulin are used to treat high K for this reason
Out of cells: acidosis, cell lysis, digoxin, beta-blockers, insulin lack

stem: A 32-year-old woman who lives at sea level takes acetazolamide before a trek to high altitude. Four hours after the first dose her spot urine is tested.
oneliner: 32F + acetazolamide before altitude trek + urine tested 4 h after first dose → expected urine change?
ask: Which urine finding is expected?

options.A: Acidic pH, increased bicarbonate, increased volume
options.B: Alkaline pH, increased bicarbonate, increased volume
options.C: Alkaline pH, decreased bicarbonate, decreased volume
options.D: Acidic pH, decreased bicarbonate, decreased volume
options.E: Neutral pH, normal bicarbonate, decreased volume

whyNot.A: Bicarbonate is lost, so the urine becomes **alkaline**, not acidic
whyNot.C: **Bicarbonate in urine rises**; sodium and water follow it, raising volume
whyNot.D: Reabsorption is blocked, so urine bicarbonate is **high**
whyNot.E: Drug is a **diuretic**, so volume increases

answer: Bicarbonate diuresis: alkaline, bicarbonate-rich, larger-volume urine
why: **Carbonic anhydrase inhibition** in the **proximal tubule** stops **bicarbonate reabsorption**. Bicarbonate, with **sodium and water**, stays in the urine (**alkaline diuresis**) and a **metabolic acidosis** results, which drives breathing at altitude.
chain: Less HCO3- reabsorbed in proximal tubule

idea.rule: Acetazolamide causes bicarbonate diuresis and metabolic acidosis; the acidosis stimulates breathing.
also: Used for altitude sickness, glaucoma, pseudotumor cerebri, alkalinization
Adverse effects: hyperchloremic acidosis, hypokalemia, paresthesias, sulfa allergy
Alkaline urine helps clear salicylates and uric acid

stem: A 72-year-old man has had nocturia, hesitancy, and a weak stream for 3 years, and now has fever and dysuria. The prostate is smooth, symmetric, and enlarged. Postvoid residual volume is 300 mL. Ultrasound shows a thick-walled bladder with a diverticulum and dilated renal pelvises on both sides. There are no stones on CT, the retroperitoneum is normal, and fasting glucose is normal.
oneliner: 72M + 3 y nocturia, hesitancy, weak stream + smooth enlarged prostate + residual 300 mL + thick bladder, diverticulum + bilateral hydronephrosis + no stones, normal retroperitoneum and glucose + UTI → why bilateral hydronephrosis?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the hydronephrosis?

options.A: Chronic outlet obstruction raising bladder pressure that is transmitted back to the kidneys
options.B: Bilateral ureteral stones
options.C: Retroperitoneal fibrosis encasing both ureters
options.D: Diabetic bladder with loss of sensation

whyNot.C: The **retroperitoneum is normal** on CT
whyNot.D: Needs **diabetes**; his glucose is normal and he has a prostate cause
whyNot.E: Presents in **childhood** with recurrent UTI; he has a clear outlet obstruction

answer: Prostatic outlet obstruction with back-pressure on the upper tracts
why: An **enlarged prostate narrows the urethra**, so the bladder wall **hypertrophies and forms diverticula**. Residual urine and **high intravesical pressure** are **transmitted up the ureters**, causing **bilateral hydronephrosis** and **infection from stasis**.

idea.rule: Bilateral hydronephrosis in an older man with a big prostate means bladder outlet obstruction until proven otherwise.
also: Posterior urethral valves do the same in male infants
Chronic obstruction can cause post-renal failure
Urine stasis predisposes to UTI and stones

stem: A 27-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation has had 2 days of fever, shaking chills and right flank pain. Temperature is 39.2°C and there is marked right costovertebral angle tenderness. She has no heart murmur and no other site of infection. A photomicrograph of the affected kidney is shown.
oneliner: 27F + 32 weeks pregnant + fever, chills + right flank pain and CVA tenderness + kidney histology shown → how did the infection arrive?
ask: Which of the following best explains how this infection reached the kidney?

options.A: Bloodborne seeding from a distant focus
options.B: Bladder bacteria ascended because ureteral dilation caused urine stasis
options.C: Spread from an infected uterine cavity

whyNot.A: **Hematogenous** spread follows bacteremia from a distant focus (e.g. endocarditis); she has **no murmur and no other infection site**
whyNot.C: **Chorioamnionitis** gives uterine tenderness and fetal tachycardia, not isolated flank pain
whyNot.D: **PID** gives lower abdominal and cervical motion tenderness and is rare at 32 weeks
whyNot.E: No bowel symptoms; lymphatic spread to the kidney is not a usual route

answer: Ureteral dilation and urine stasis allow ascending infection
why: **Progesterone relaxes ureteral smooth muscle** and the **gravid uterus compresses the ureters** (more on the right). The dilated, stagnant system lets bacteria **ascend** from the bladder to the renal pelvis.
chain: Progesterone and the uterus dilate and compress the ureters

idea.rule: Pregnancy dilates the ureters, and stasis promotes ascending infection.
also: Pyelonephritis is more common on the right (uterine dextrorotation)
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is screened for and treated in pregnancy
Any urinary stasis (stones, BPH, neurogenic bladder) raises UTI risk

image.prompt: H&E photomicrograph of kidney: renal tubules whose lumens are packed with neutrophils and neutrophil casts, with neutrophils infiltrating the interstitium; glomeruli look unaffected. No text or labels.

stem: A 71-year-old man has had 6 months of a weak urinary stream and nocturia, and now feels tired. His creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 4.0 mg/dL. Ultrasonography shows bilateral hydronephrosis and a bladder that still holds a large volume after voiding.
oneliner: 71M + weak stream + creatinine 1.1→4.0 + bilateral hydronephrosis + large residual urine → why has GFR fallen?
ask: Which change most directly accounts for the fall in his glomerular filtration rate?

options.A: Increased hydrostatic pressure in Bowman space
options.B: Increased glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure
options.C: Decreased glomerular capillary oncotic pressure

whyNot.B: That would **raise** filtration, not lower it
whyNot.C: That would **raise** net filtration pressure
whyNot.D: Acts on **reabsorption** after filtration, not on GFR
whyNot.E: Would need afferent constriction or low perfusion; urine is **backed up** here, not underperfused

answer: Obstruction raises Bowman space pressure, which opposes filtration
why: Outflow obstruction (here prostatic) makes urine **back up to the nephron**. **Bowman space hydrostatic pressure rises** and opposes the push out of the capillary, so net filtration pressure and GFR fall.
chain: Urine backs up into the tubules

idea.rule: GFR depends on net filtration pressure: glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure minus (Bowman space pressure + capillary oncotic pressure).
also: Afferent arteriole constriction (NSAIDs) lowers glomerular pressure and GFR
Efferent arteriole dilation (ACE inhibitors) lowers glomerular pressure and GFR
Low plasma protein lowers oncotic pressure and raises filtration
Stones, BPH, tumors and strictures raise Bowman space pressure

stem: A 52-year-old woman has had 6 weeks of tiredness and nausea, with vaginal spotting after intercourse. Creatinine is 5.2 mg/dL and BUN 64 mg/dL. Ultrasonography shows hydronephrosis and hydroureter on both sides, and the bladder is empty.
oneliner: 52F + postcoital spotting + creatinine 5.2 + bilateral hydroureter and hydronephrosis + empty bladder → which organ's tumor?
ask: A tumor arising in which of the following structures most likely caused the kidney failure?

options.A: Ovary
options.B: Sigmoid colon
options.C: Uterine cervix

whyNot.A: **Ovarian cancer** brings bloating and ascites, not postcoital bleeding
whyNot.B: **Colon cancer** presents with bowel habit change or rectal bleeding
whyNot.D: A primary **renal tumor** is usually unilateral with hematuria, and would not dilate both ureters
whyNot.E: **Urothelial ureteral tumor** is usually unilateral and causes hematuria

answer: Cervical carcinoma spreads laterally and compresses both ureters
why: **Postcoital bleeding** points to the **cervix**. Cervical carcinoma spreads laterally into the parametria and **encases both ureters**, producing bilateral obstruction and **postrenal azotemia**.
chain: Cervical carcinoma spreads into the parametria
Both ureters compressed at the pelvic brim

idea.rule: A pelvic tumor that spreads sideways can trap both ureters and cause postrenal kidney failure.
also: Cervical cancer: ureteral obstruction with uremia is a common cause of death
Bladder cancer invading both ureteral orifices
Retroperitoneal fibrosis encasing the ureters
Bladder outlet obstruction (BPH) also dilates both sides, but the bladder is full

stem: A 42-year-old man has had 3 weeks of swelling around the eyes and in both legs. Blood pressure is normal. His neck veins are flat and there is no third heart sound. Urine dipstick shows 4+ protein, and a 24-hour collection contains 15 g of protein.
oneliner: 42M + periorbital and leg swelling + normal BP and neck veins + 15 g protein/day → why the edema?
ask: Which of the following best explains his edema?

options.A: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure
options.B: Decreased capillary hydrostatic pressure
options.C: Increased venular permeability
options.E: Raised venous pressure from heart failure

whyNot.B: That would **pull fluid in**, the opposite of edema
whyNot.C: Seen with **histamine or inflammation** (urticaria, angioedema), not with proteinuria
whyNot.D: Causes **nonpitting, localized** edema (filariasis, surgery)
whyNot.E: Would show **raised neck veins and an S3**, which he lacks

answer: Albumin loss lowers oncotic pressure, so fluid leaves the capillaries
why: **Massive proteinuria** (over 3.5 g/day) lowers serum **albumin**. In the Starling equation, low **plasma oncotic pressure** lets fluid leave the capillaries into the interstitium.

idea.rule: Edema comes from raised capillary pressure, low oncotic pressure, leaky vessels or blocked lymph; in nephrotic syndrome it is low oncotic pressure.
also: Liver failure: less albumin made
Protein-losing enteropathy
Severe protein malnutrition (kwashiorkor)

stem: A 66-year-old man with heart failure and long-standing kidney disease has nausea and deep, rapid breathing. Labs: Na 138, K 5.6, Cl 100, HCO3 12 mEq/L, BUN 100 and creatinine 8.4 mg/dL. Arterial pH is 7.21 and PaCO2 is 26 mm Hg. Serum ketones and lactate are normal, he does not drink alcohol, and he has no diarrhea.
oneliner: 66M + HF and kidney disease + deep breathing + HCO3 12, anion gap 26 + BUN 100, Cr 8.4 + normal ketones and lactate → why acidotic?
ask: Which of the following best explains his acid-base disturbance?

options.A: Insulin deficiency with ketoacid overproduction
options.B: Failure of the kidneys to excrete acid and regenerate bicarbonate
options.C: Metabolism of ethanol with NADH excess

whyNot.A: **DKA**: serum ketones are normal here
whyNot.C: **Alcoholic ketoacidosis**: history of heavy drinking and ketones
whyNot.D: **Milk-alkali** causes metabolic **alkalosis**, with high bicarbonate
whyNot.E: **Diarrhea** gives a **normal** anion gap acidosis; he has none and his gap is 26

answer: Loss of nephron mass causes acid retention and bicarbonate loss
why: Gap = 138 − (100 + 12) = **26**, so unmeasured anions are retained. With **creatinine 8.4**, the failing nephrons cannot **excrete acid (ammonium, phosphate, sulfate)** or make new bicarbonate, giving a **high anion gap metabolic acidosis**.
chain: Acid excretion and bicarbonate regeneration fall
Sulfate, phosphate and urate anions accumulate

idea.rule: Advanced renal failure causes a high anion gap acidosis because the kidney cannot excrete acid anions or make new bicarbonate.
also: Moderate CKD often gives a normal anion gap acidosis first
Retained anions: sulfate, phosphate, urate
Uremia is the U in MUDPILES

stem: A 61-year-old man has an adrenal mass that partly compresses his right renal artery, lowering the mean pressure beyond it from 100 to 85 mmHg. Right renal plasma flow, GFR and filtration fraction are all the same as on the left.
oneliner: 61M + mass compressing right renal artery + pressure beyond it 100 → 85 mmHg + renal plasma flow, GFR and filtration fraction all unchanged → what keeps them steady?
ask: Which change in the right kidney most likely keeps both plasma flow and GFR constant?

options.A: Dilation of the afferent arteriole
options.B: Constriction of the efferent arteriole
options.C: Constriction of both afferent and efferent arterioles

whyNot.B: Would hold GFR but **cut plasma flow and raise filtration fraction**; both are unchanged here
whyNot.C: Raises resistance, so it would **cut plasma flow**, which is unchanged
whyNot.D: **Lowers glomerular capillary pressure**, so GFR and filtration fraction would fall
whyNot.E: Surface area does not change quickly and **would not hold plasma flow**; it is not the autoregulatory response

answer: Afferent arteriolar dilation (myogenic reflex and tubuloglomerular feedback)
why: The pressure fall stays **within the autoregulatory range**, so the **afferent arteriole relaxes** (myogenic response; less NaCl at the macula densa adds feedback dilation). Lower resistance upstream restores both **plasma flow and glomerular pressure**, so GFR and **filtration fraction stay unchanged**; efferent constriction would have raised filtration fraction.
chain: Afferent wall stretches less, myogenic relaxation
Less NaCl at macula densa, feedback dilation

idea.rule: Autoregulation (about 80-180 mmHg) keeps both renal plasma flow and GFR steady by adjusting afferent tone.
also: Pressure rises: afferent constricts (myogenic response)
Tubuloglomerular feedback: more NaCl at macula densa, adenosine, afferent constriction
Below about 80 mmHg flow falls; angiotensin II efferent constriction then holds GFR and filtration fraction rises

stem: In an anesthetized rat, a clamp narrows one renal artery so that the mean pressure beyond it falls from 100 to 60 mmHg. On that side renal plasma flow falls by 25%, GFR is unchanged, and the filtration fraction rises.
oneliner: Rat + renal artery clamped, pressure 100 → 60 mmHg + plasma flow −25% + GFR unchanged + filtration fraction up → which change preserves GFR?
ask: Which change in the clamped kidney best explains the preserved GFR?

options.A: Constriction of the afferent arteriole
options.B: Dilation of the afferent arteriole
options.C: Constriction of the efferent arteriole

whyNot.A: Would **lower glomerular pressure further** and reduce GFR
whyNot.B: Would raise flow and GFR together: **filtration fraction would stay the same**, but here plasma flow fell and filtration fraction rose
whyNot.D: Would **drop glomerular capillary pressure**, and filtration fraction would fall, not rise
whyNot.E: Would **reduce** GFR, not preserve it

answer: Efferent arteriolar constriction (angiotensin II)
why: Falling perfusion pressure raises **renin and angiotensin II**, which **constricts the efferent arteriole** preferentially. Glomerular pressure is kept up, so **GFR holds while plasma flow falls**, which is why **filtration fraction rises**.
chain: Plasma flow falls, filtration fraction rises

idea.rule: Efferent constriction preserves GFR at the price of lower plasma flow, so filtration fraction rises.
also: ACE inhibitors or ARBs in bilateral renal artery stenosis: GFR drops, creatinine rises
Volume depletion or heart failure: angiotensin II raises filtration fraction
Prerenal azotemia: BUN/creatinine above 20 as more urea is reabsorbed

stem: A 12-year-old girl has had 2 weeks of thirst, frequent urination and weight loss. Serum glucose is 350 mg/dL and urine dipstick shows 4+ glucose. Her creatinine is normal, and her urine has no excess amino acids or phosphate.
oneliner: 12F + 2 wk thirst, polyuria, weight loss + glucose 350 + urine glucose 4+ + normal creatinine, no aminoaciduria or phosphaturia → why glucose in urine?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the glucosuria?

options.A: Reduced expression of SGLT transporters
options.B: Filtered glucose load exceeds the proximal tubule transport maximum
options.C: Loss of the sodium gradient that powers glucose entry into tubular cells
options.D: Impaired GLUT2 exit across the basolateral membrane

whyNot.A: Would give glucosuria at **normal blood glucose**; hers is 350
whyNot.C: Would need **Na+/K+-ATPase failure** with wider tubular damage; nothing suggests it, and her glucose load alone explains the spill
whyNot.D: A GLUT2 defect (**Fanconi–Bickel**) gives glucosuria with **low or normal** blood glucose, plus aminoaciduria and phosphaturia
whyNot.E: Would also waste **amino acids and phosphate**, which are normal here

answer: Saturation of tubular glucose reabsorption (SGLT) by hyperglycemia
why: **Hyperglycemia pushes filtered glucose above the transport maximum** of proximal tubule **SGLT2/SGLT1**. The unreabsorbed glucose spills into urine and **drags water with it (osmotic diuresis)**, causing the polyuria.

idea.rule: Glucosuria with high blood glucose is saturation; glucosuria with normal blood glucose is a transporter defect.
also: Renal glycosuria: SGLT2 mutation, normal glucose
SGLT2 inhibitors cause glucosuria on purpose
Pregnancy lowers the threshold slightly

stem: A 2-year-old boy has poor growth, excessive urination, photophobia and bowed legs. Urine contains glucose, phosphate and amino acids, and blood shows pH 7.28, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L and a normal anion gap, with a urine pH of 4.9. Serum glucose and potassium are normal.
oneliner: 2M + poor growth + polyuria + photophobia + bowed legs + glucosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria + non-anion-gap acidosis, urine pH 4.9 + normal serum glucose and K → mechanism of the acidosis?
ask: Which mechanism best explains his acidosis?

options.A: Failure of H+ secretion by distal intercalated cells
options.B: Reduced bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
options.C: Reduced carbonic anhydrase activity in the distal tubule

whyNot.A: Would give **urine pH above 5.3**; his urine pH is 4.9
whyNot.C: Would also be a distal defect with a **high urine pH**
whyNot.D: Would give **hyperkalemia** (his potassium is normal) and does not waste glucose, phosphate and amino acids
whyNot.E: Would raise the **anion gap**, which is normal here

answer: Proximal tubule dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome) wasting bicarbonate: type 2 renal tubular acidosis
why: **Glucose, phosphate and amino acids in urine with normal blood glucose** mean the **proximal tubule** is failing as a whole. It also **loses bicarbonate**, causing a **normal-anion-gap acidosis**; the distal nephron still acidifies (**urine pH 4.9**). With photophobia from corneal crystals, this fits **cystinosis**.
chain: Lysosomal cystine builds up in tubular cells
Glucose, phosphate, amino acids and HCO3- wasted

idea.rule: A generalized proximal tubule defect wastes everything the proximal tubule reabsorbs, including bicarbonate.
also: Wilson disease, heavy metals, tenofovir, multiple myeloma
Type 1 RTA: distal, urine pH above 5.3
Type 4 RTA: hypoaldosteronism, high K

stem: A 19-year-old man with sickle cell disease has severe flank pain and gross hematuria during a pain crisis. Urinalysis shows red cells with no white cell casts, and CT shows no stones or masses.
oneliner: 19M + sickle cell disease in crisis + flank pain + gross hematuria + no WBC casts + no stones or mass on CT → why bleeding from the kidney?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the hematuria?

options.A: Immune complex deposition in glomeruli
options.B: Sickling in the hypoxic, hypertonic medulla blocks the vasa recta and infarcts the papillae
options.C: Invasion by urothelial carcinoma

whyNot.A: Would give **RBC casts and proteinuria**, not gross bleeding with flank pain
whyNot.C: **CT shows no mass**
whyNot.D: **CT shows no stones**
whyNot.E: Would give **fever and WBC casts**; none seen

answer: Renal papillary necrosis from medullary ischemia
why: The **renal medulla is low in oxygen and very hypertonic**, which favors **sickling**. Sickled cells **plug the vasa recta**, the **papillae infarct and slough**, causing **hematuria and flank pain**.
chain: Low oxygen and high osmolarity in medulla

idea.rule: Papillae are the watershed of the kidney: ischemia there causes necrosis.
also: Analgesic (NSAID) nephropathy
Diabetes mellitus
Acute pyelonephritis
Obstruction (mnemonic POSTED)

stem: A 38-year-old woman has had repeated urinary tract infections and now has right flank pain. Urine pH is 8.0, with hematuria and pyuria, and a urine culture grows Proteus mirabilis. CT shows a branching stone filling the renal pelvis.
oneliner: 38F + recurrent UTIs + flank pain + urine pH 8.0 + Proteus + branching renal pelvis stone → mechanism of stone?
ask: Which of the following best explains stone formation?

options.A: Bacterial splitting of urea, raising urine pH
options.B: Excess intestinal oxalate absorption
options.C: Increased urinary uric acid
options.D: Defective tubular reabsorption of dibasic amino acids

whyNot.B: Causes **calcium oxalate** stones in acidic or neutral urine, not a pH of 8
whyNot.C: Forms in **acidic** urine, radiolucent, in gout or high cell turnover
whyNot.D: **Cystine** stones form in **acidic** urine without infection; hers is pH 8 with Proteus
whyNot.E: Would make calcium stones in **normal or acidic** urine with no infection

answer: Urease-producing bacteria split urea to ammonia, alkalinising urine, so struvite precipitates
why: **Urease-producing** organisms (*Proteus*, *Klebsiella*) convert urea to **ammonia**, raising urine pH. **Magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite)** precipitates in alkaline urine, often as a **staghorn** stone.

idea.rule: Urine pH and solute decide which stone forms; urease organisms alkalinise urine and give struvite.
also: Calcium oxalate: most common, envelope crystals
Uric acid: acidic urine, radiolucent
Cystine: hexagonal crystals, positive nitroprusside
Stones harbour bacteria, so cure needs removal

stem: A 34-year-old woman has had recurrent urinary tract infections since childhood. She now has hypertension, proteinuria, and a creatinine of 3.1 mg/dL. She has no diabetes and takes no analgesics. A nephrectomy specimen is shown.
oneliner: 34F + UTIs since childhood + hypertension + proteinuria + renal insufficiency + no diabetes or analgesic use + kidney specimen → how did this injury arise?
ask: Which of the following most likely produced the changes in this kidney?

options.A: Ischemic necrosis of the renal papillae from analgesics
options.B: Glomerular sclerosis from long-standing hyperglycemia
options.C: Backflow of infected urine into the kidney with scarring at the poles
options.D: Deposition of amyloid in the interstitium
options.E: Deposition of immune complexes in glomerular capillaries

whyNot.A: She takes **no analgesics**; papillary necrosis would not give polar cortical scars
whyNot.D: Would give a **large, waxy** kidney, not scars
whyNot.E: Would give **nephritic or nephrotic** features with a smooth kidney, not scars and infections

answer: Vesicoureteral reflux with recurrent infection, leading to polar scarring (reflux nephropathy)
why: **Vesicoureteral reflux** carries infected urine into the kidney (**intrarenal reflux**, especially into the compound papillae at the **poles**). Repeated infection produces **coarse scars with calyceal blunting**, then hypertension, proteinuria (**FSGS**) and chronic kidney disease.

idea.rule: Polar scars with blunted calyces suggest reflux nephropathy.
also: Compound papillae at the poles allow intrarenal reflux
Coarse corticomedullary scar over a blunted calyx = chronic pyelonephritis
Thyroidization of tubules on histology
Secondary FSGS from nephron loss

image.prompt: Gross photograph of a bisected kidney with coarse, irregular, depressed scars overlying the upper and lower poles, thinned cortex beneath the scars, and blunted, dilated calyces. Neutral background. No text or labels.

stem: A 44-year-old man had a kidney transplant 3 months ago. He now has a rising creatinine (1.2 to 2.6 mg/dL) and mild hypertension. He admits missing several doses of tacrolimus, and the trough level is low. Biopsy shows lymphocytes within the tubules and in the walls of small arteries.
oneliner: 44M + kidney transplant 3 mo + creatinine 1.2 to 2.6 + missed tacrolimus, low trough + biopsy: lymphocytes in tubules and arterial walls → mechanism?
ask: Which of the following best explains the graft dysfunction?

options.A: Thrombosis from preformed antibodies
options.B: Deposition of donor-specific antibody and complement in capillaries
options.C: Vasoconstriction from calcineurin inhibitor toxicity
options.D: Recipient T cells attacking donor antigens in tubules and vessels
options.E: Slow intimal thickening and fibrosis of graft vessels

whyNot.A: That is **hyperacute** rejection, minutes to hours after transplant
whyNot.B: Antibody-mediated rejection shows **capillaritis and C4d**, not lymphocytes in tubules
whyNot.C: His tacrolimus level is **low**, and the biopsy shows lymphocytes
whyNot.E: That is **chronic** rejection, after months to years, with little inflammation

answer: Acute T-cell mediated rejection
why: Under-immunosuppression lets **recipient T cells recognize donor MHC** and infiltrate the graft, producing **tubulitis and endarteritis**. This **acute cellular rejection** appears **weeks to months** after transplant and responds to **more immunosuppression**.
chain: Recipient T cells recognize donor MHC

idea.rule: Rejection type is set by timing and effector; T cells in tubules and vessels weeks to months later = acute cellular rejection.
also: Hyperacute: preformed antibody, minutes
Acute humoral: DSA, C4d
Chronic: fibrosis, vasculopathy, years
Treat acute cellular rejection with steroids

stem: A 60-year-old man with long-standing diabetic kidney disease and an eGFR of 12 mL/min has itching with scratch marks, nausea, little urine and easy gum bleeding. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL with an MCV of 88 fL. Serum albumin is 4.0 g/dL, TSH and prothrombin time are normal, and he eats fresh fruit daily.
oneliner: 60M + diabetic CKD eGFR 12 + pruritus with excoriations + nausea + oliguria + gum bleeding + Hb 8.9, MCV 88 + normal albumin, TSH, PT + eats fruit → mechanism?
ask: Which of the following best explains his findings?

options.A: Low oncotic pressure from protein loss
options.B: Slowed marrow and skin turnover from low thyroid hormone
options.C: Defective collagen hydroxylation from vitamin C lack
options.E: Retained uremic toxins with low erythropoietin output

whyNot.A: His **albumin is 4.0**, which is normal
whyNot.C: He **eats fresh fruit daily**
whyNot.D: **Prothrombin time is normal**

answer: Uremia: failing kidneys retain toxins and make less erythropoietin
why: With eGFR near 12, the kidneys cannot excrete **nitrogenous toxins (uremia)**, causing **pruritus, nausea and platelet dysfunction** (bleeding). Damaged interstitial cells make less **erythropoietin**, giving **normocytic anemia**.
chain: Urea, guanidines and other toxins accumulate

idea.rule: Advanced CKD: uremic symptoms plus normocytic anemia from low EPO.
also: Uremic pericarditis, encephalopathy, asterixis
Treat anemia with erythropoietin
Bleeding corrected by dialysis or desmopressin
Hyperphosphatemia and low calcium cause secondary hyperparathyroidism

stem: A 29-year-old woman has a blood pressure of 168/104 mm Hg found at a routine visit. An abdominal bruit is heard on the left. Serum potassium is 3.1 mEq/L and bicarbonate is 31 mEq/L. Plasma renin activity and aldosterone are both raised, and renin rises further after captopril. She has no virilization and no episodes of headache, sweating or palpitations.
oneliner: 29F + BP 168/104 + abdominal bruit + K 3.1 + HCO3 31 + high renin and high aldosterone, renin higher after captopril → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains her hypertension?

options.A: Autonomous aldosterone secretion by an adrenal adenoma
options.B: Low renal perfusion pressure driving renin release
options.C: Excess cortisol saturating the mineralocorticoid receptor
options.E: Catecholamine surge from a chromaffin tumor

whyNot.A: **Conn syndrome**: aldosterone high but **renin suppressed**
whyNot.C: **Cushing**: renin low, with central obesity and striae
whyNot.D: Renin **low**, and virilization would be expected; she has none
whyNot.E: **Pheochromocytoma**: episodic headache, sweating and palpitations; she has **none**, and it does not explain the bruit

answer: Renal artery stenosis reduces perfusion and activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
why: A stenotic renal artery makes the kidney sense **low perfusion pressure**, so the juxtaglomerular cells release **renin**. **Angiotensin II and aldosterone** raise pressure and waste potassium, causing **hypokalemic alkalosis**. Captopril removes negative feedback, so renin rises more.

idea.rule: High renin with high aldosterone = secondary hyperaldosteronism.
also: Primary aldosteronism: high aldosterone, low renin
Fibromuscular dysplasia: young women, beaded renal artery
ACE inhibitors can drop GFR in bilateral stenosis

stem: A 38-year-old woman collapses after finishing a marathon. She drank at every aid station and weighed 2 kg more at the finish than at the start. She is confused, then has a generalized seizure. Serum sodium is 116 mEq/L, serum osmolality is low, and urine osmolality is 480 mOsm/kg.
oneliner: 38F + marathon + drank at every station + gained 2 kg + confusion and seizure + Na 116 + low serum osm + urine osm 480 → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains her sodium?

options.A: Sodium loss in sweat without any water retention
options.B: Suppressed ADH with excess urinary water loss
options.C: Aldosterone deficiency with renal sodium wasting
options.D: Water intake exceeding water excretion, diluting plasma sodium
options.E: Osmotic shift of water from high blood glucose

whyNot.A: Sweat loss alone would give **weight loss**; she **gained** weight
whyNot.B: Urine would be **dilute** and she would lose weight; her urine osm is 480
whyNot.C: Would cause **hypovolemia and hyperkalemia**, with weight loss
whyNot.E: Glucose is not raised and **serum osmolality is low**, not high

answer: Water overload with non-osmotic ADH: plasma dilution and cerebral edema
why: She **gained weight** by drinking more water than she lost, and exercise-related **non-osmotic ADH** release stops her excreting it. **Plasma sodium is diluted** and water enters brain cells, causing **cerebral edema**, confusion and seizure.

idea.rule: Low sodium with weight gain = too much water retained, not too little salt.
also: Exercise-associated hyponatremia: drinking beyond losses with non-osmotic ADH
SIADH: water retained, euvolemic, concentrated urine
Beer potomania and tea-and-toast diet: too little solute to excrete the water drunk

stem: A 44-year-old woman who has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for 9 years has passed about 6 liters of urine daily and is constantly thirsty. Serum osmolality is 315 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality is 75 mOsm/kg, and glucose is normal. Urine osmolality stays at 78 mOsm/kg after desmopressin. She takes no diuretics.
oneliner: 44F + lithium 9 y + polyuria 6 L/day + serum osm 315 + urine osm 75 + no rise after desmopressin + normal glucose → defect?
ask: Which defect best explains her urine?

options.A: Failure of ADH release from the posterior pituitary
options.B: Impaired ADH signaling in collecting duct cells, so aquaporin-2 is not inserted
options.C: Osmotic diuresis from glucose
options.E: Blockade of the loop of Henle sodium transporter

whyNot.A: **Central DI** responds to desmopressin by concentrating urine
whyNot.C: Glucose is normal and urine would be **concentrated**, not dilute
whyNot.D: **Primary polydipsia**: serum osmolality is **low**, not 315
whyNot.E: She takes **no loop diuretic** and urine osm would be about 300, not 75

answer: Lithium blocks the cAMP pathway in principal cells, so aquaporin-2 channels are not inserted
why: Lithium enters principal cells through ENaC and **blocks ADH-driven cAMP signaling**, so **aquaporin-2 is not inserted**. The collecting duct stays waterproof, giving **dilute urine despite hyperosmolar serum** and **no response to desmopressin**.

idea.rule: No response to desmopressin means the collecting duct, not the pituitary, is resistant.
also: Hypercalcemia and hypokalemia also blunt the collecting duct response to ADH
Demeclocycline causes it (used on purpose in SIADH)
Congenital: X-linked V2 receptor or aquaporin-2 gene mutations

stem: A 31-year-old man runs a half-marathon in hot weather and takes no fluids. Afterward he passes a small volume of very dark urine. Serum sodium is 148 mEq/L and plasma osmolality is 306 mOsm/kg H₂O. Urine osmolality is 920 mOsm/kg H₂O.
oneliner: 31M + half-marathon in heat, no fluids + small dark urine + Na 148, plasma osm 306 + urine osm 920 → why concentrated urine?
ask: Which of the following best explains his urine concentration?

options.A: Increased ANP reducing collecting duct water permeability
options.B: Decreased ADH with reduced aquaporin-2 expression
options.C: Increased ADH acting on V2 receptors to insert aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct
options.E: Increased ADH acting on V1 receptors to constrict afferent arterioles

whyNot.A: ANP **opposes** ADH and would dilute urine
whyNot.B: Gives **dilute** urine, as in diabetes insipidus
whyNot.D: Aldosterone acts on **sodium and potassium** transport, not aquaporin-2
whyNot.E: V1 receptors cause **vascular constriction**; urine concentration is a **V2** effect

answer: ADH-mediated aquaporin-2 insertion
why: Sweat loses more water than salt, so **plasma osmolality rises** and osmoreceptors release **ADH**. At **V2 receptors (Gs, cAMP)** ADH inserts **aquaporin-2** in the collecting duct, so free water is reclaimed and urine is concentrated.
chain: Sweat water loss exceeds salt loss
V2 receptor: Gs, cAMP, aquaporin-2 insertion

idea.rule: Hyperosmolality or hypovolemia triggers ADH, which adds aquaporin-2 to concentrate urine.
also: Water deprivation
Hypernatremia
Hemorrhage (volume-driven ADH)
SIADH (inappropriate ADH, concentrated urine with hyponatremia)

stem: In an anesthetized dog, the efferent arteriole of one nephron is partly constricted while the afferent arteriole and arterial pressure are held constant. Pressures are measured in the glomerular capillary.
oneliner: Dog + efferent arteriole partly constricted + afferent arteriole and arterial pressure constant → glomerular effect?
ask: Which change is expected?

options.A: Lower glomerular hydrostatic pressure and lower GFR
options.B: Higher renal plasma flow and lower filtration fraction
options.C: Unchanged glomerular pressure with higher renal plasma flow
options.D: Higher glomerular hydrostatic pressure and filtration fraction
options.E: Lower plasma oncotic pressure in the glomerular capillary

whyNot.A: Pressure **rises** behind the clamp; this describes **afferent** constriction
whyNot.B: Flow through the nephron is **restricted**, so plasma flow falls and filtration fraction rises
whyNot.C: Narrowed outflow with unchanged inflow resistance **cannot leave pressure unchanged**
whyNot.E: Oncotic pressure **rises** as more fluid is filtered out of the same plasma

answer: Increased glomerular hydrostatic pressure and filtration fraction
why: Narrowing the **efferent** arteriole makes blood back up in the glomerulus, so **hydrostatic pressure rises** and GFR rises. Plasma flow out falls, so **filtration fraction (GFR/RPF) increases**.
chain: Blood backs up in the glomerulus
GFR up, renal plasma flow down

idea.rule: Efferent constriction raises GFR and filtration fraction; afferent constriction lowers both GFR and RPF.
also: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole preferentially
ACE inhibitors dilate it and lower GFR in renal artery stenosis
Early renal artery stenosis is kept up by efferent tone

stem: A 28-year-old healthy woman has renal oxygen consumption measured by renal artery and vein sampling.
oneliner: 28F + healthy + renal O2 consumption measured → greatest user of oxygen?
ask: Which process accounts for most of the oxygen the kidneys consume?

options.A: Glomerular ultrafiltration of plasma
options.B: Synthesis of renal hormones
options.C: Excretion of titratable acid

whyNot.A: Filtration is **passive**, driven by hydrostatic pressure
whyNot.B: Hormone production is a **small** metabolic load
whyNot.C: Acid excretion is a **minor** consumer
whyNot.D: Gluconeogenesis uses some energy but is **far smaller** than sodium transport

answer: Tubular sodium reabsorption
why: Most renal oxygen goes to **Na+/K+-ATPase** on the basolateral membrane, which powers sodium reabsorption. Renal oxygen use therefore **tracks sodium reabsorption**, not filtration.

idea.rule: Renal oxygen consumption is set by active sodium transport, which rises and falls with GFR.
also: Loop diuretics lower renal O2 use by cutting Na+ reabsorption
The medullary thick ascending limb, a heavy Na+ transporter, is the most hypoxia-prone segment
A fall in GFR lowers filtered Na+ and renal O2 use

stem: A 30-year-old man feels the urge to void when his bladder holds about 400 mL. He relaxes the pelvic floor and the bladder wall contracts, raising intravesical pressure until urine flows.
oneliner: 30M + urge at 400 mL + relaxes pelvic floor + bladder contracts and he voids → efferent pathway for the contraction?
ask: Which outflow produces the bladder wall contraction?

options.A: Sympathetic hypogastric nerve outflow
options.B: Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic outflow
options.C: Somatic pudendal nerve outflow

whyNot.A: Sympathetic input **relaxes the detrusor** and contracts the internal sphincter (storage)
whyNot.C: The pudendal nerve controls the **external sphincter**, which he relaxed
whyNot.D: The vagus does not reach the bladder; pelvic organs use **sacral** outflow
whyNot.E: Cortex only **permits** voiding via the pontine center; it does not supply the detrusor

answer: Sacral parasympathetic (S2-S4) outflow
why: The **pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4)** are parasympathetic and cause **detrusor contraction** and sphincter relaxation. Sympathetic and pudendal outflow serve storage and continence.

idea.rule: Parasympathetic S2-S4 empties; sympathetic stores; somatic (pudendal) holds voluntarily.
also: Sympathetic hypogastric (T11-L2): detrusor relaxes, internal sphincter contracts during filling
Pudendal (S2-S4): voluntary external sphincter hold
Sacral cord injury: loss of S2-S4 outflow gives an atonic overflow bladder

stem: In a micropuncture study in rats, the amount of filtered bicarbonate remaining is measured along successive nephron segments.
oneliner: Rat micropuncture + tracking filtered bicarbonate along the nephron → which segment takes the largest share?
ask: In which segment is most filtered bicarbonate reabsorbed?

options.A: Proximal convoluted tubule
options.B: Distal convoluted tubule
options.C: Collecting duct

whyNot.C: Reclaims only the **last few percent** and mainly secretes H+ to acidify the urine
whyNot.E: Has **no** meaningful bicarbonate reabsorption
whyNot.D: Takes up about **10-15%**, not the bulk

answer: Proximal convoluted tubule
why: The **proximal tubule** reabsorbs about **80-85%** of filtered bicarbonate. Luminal H+ (via NHE3) combines with HCO3-, and **brush-border carbonic anhydrase** converts it to CO2 for entry.
chain: NHE3 secretes H+ into the lumen
CO2 enters and is rebuilt to HCO3-
HCO3- leaves across the basolateral side

idea.rule: Most bicarbonate reabsorption occurs in the proximal tubule and needs carbonic anhydrase.
also: Acetazolamide blocks it and causes bicarbonate loss
Type 2 (proximal) RTA is a defect here
Proximal tubule also reabsorbs most glucose and amino acids

stem: A healthy 26-year-old man drinks 1 L of water over 1 hour. His plasma osmolality falls from 290 to 282 mOsm/kg. Plasma ADH, urine osmolality, and urine flow are measured over the next two hours.
oneliner: 26M + drinks 1 L water + plasma osm 290 to 282 → ADH, urine osmolality, urine flow?
ask: Which pattern is expected?

options.A: ADH higher, urine osmolality higher, urine flow lower
options.B: ADH lower, urine osmolality higher, urine flow higher
options.C: ADH higher, urine osmolality lower, urine flow higher
options.D: ADH unchanged, urine osmolality lower, urine flow unchanged
options.E: ADH lower, urine osmolality lower, urine flow higher

whyNot.A: This is the pattern of **water deprivation**, not water loading
whyNot.B: Dilute urine needs **low ADH**; concentrated urine with high flow does not fit
whyNot.C: High ADH would **retain** water, not produce a flood of urine
whyNot.D: Falling osmolality **must** suppress ADH; it does not stay flat

answer: Low ADH, dilute urine, high urine flow
why: Falling plasma osmolality **switches off hypothalamic osmoreceptors**, so **ADH drops**. The collecting duct becomes water-impermeable and the kidney excretes a **large volume of dilute urine**.

idea.rule: Low plasma osmolality suppresses ADH, giving dilute urine in large volume.
also: Primary polydipsia: ADH suppressed, large dilute urine volume
Rapid hypotonic IV fluid gives the same water diuresis
Beer potomania: water load suppresses ADH, but low solute intake limits free-water excretion

stem: A healthy 35-year-old man receives 2.0 L of 0.9% saline intravenously. He passes no urine during the infusion.
oneliner: 35M + 2.0 L isotonic saline IV + no urine output yet → increase in extracellular fluid volume?
ask: By about how many liters does extracellular fluid volume increase?

whyNot.A: Would assume part of the fluid enters **cells**
whyNot.B: That is about **two thirds** of the volume; isotonic saline does not enter cells
whyNot.C: Still implies fluid **moved into cells**
whyNot.E: Cannot exceed the volume given; **no source** of extra water

why: Isotonic saline does not change plasma osmolality, so there is **no osmotic shift into cells**. All **2.0 L stays in the ECF**, split between plasma and interstitium.
chain: All 2 L stays in the ECF

idea.rule: Isotonic fluid expands only the ECF; free water spreads across all compartments.
also: Hypotonic saline moves water into cells
Hypertonic saline pulls water out of cells
D5W is distributed to total body water

stem: A 24-year-old woman has dysuria and frequency for one day. This is her third urinary infection this year, and each began within a day of sexual intercourse. She is afebrile with no flank pain, menses are regular, pregnancy test is negative, pelvic examination is normal, and she empties her bladder fully. Urine is nitrite and leukocyte esterase positive.
oneliner: 24F + 3rd UTI in a year, each after intercourse + dysuria, frequency + nitrite and LE positive + normal pelvic exam, no retention → mechanism?
ask: What most likely explains the recurrences?

options.A: A pelvic mass compressing the bladder
options.B: Perineal bacteria pushed into the urethra during intercourse
options.C: Falling estrogen thinning the urethral mucosa
options.E: Reflux from a short ureteral tunnel

whyNot.A: Pelvic examination is **normal**
whyNot.C: Menses are **regular**, so estrogen is not falling
whyNot.D: She is **not pregnant**
whyNot.E: She has no flank pain, fever, or **upper-tract** signs

answer: Bacteria carried into the short female urethra during intercourse
why: The short female urethra lies close to the vagina and perineum. **Intercourse massages colonizing bowel flora (E. coli) up the urethra** into the bladder, making it the strongest risk factor for recurrent cystitis in young women.
chain: Intercourse pushes bacteria up the urethra

idea.rule: Cystitis is ascending infection; short urethra plus mechanical introduction raises risk.
also: Diaphragm and spermicide use
Catheterization
Postmenopausal atrophy
Pregnancy

stem: A 66-year-old man has sudden left flank pain with nausea. He has no history of stones, and urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria. His pulse is irregularly irregular. A contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen is shown.
oneliner: 66M + sudden left flank pain + hematuria, irregularly irregular pulse + wedge-shaped renal defect on CT → source?
ask: What most likely caused the finding on CT?

options.A: Obstructing stone at the ureteropelvic junction
options.B: Thrombus in the renal vein
options.C: Embolus from the fibrillating left atrium
options.D: Immune complex arteritis of renal arteries
options.E: Compression of the renal artery by a cyst

whyNot.A: No stone history, and a stone gives **hydronephrosis**, not a wedge defect
whyNot.B: Vein thrombosis gives an **enlarged congested** kidney, not a peripheral wedge
whyNot.D: Arteritis gives **multiple small infarcts with systemic signs**; a single sudden event with an irregular pulse points to an embolus
whyNot.E: No cyst is described, and compression would not cause a **sudden** wedge

answer: Embolus from the left atrium in atrial fibrillation
why: A **wedge-shaped, non-enhancing** area means a **segmental renal artery branch** was occluded. With an irregular pulse, the source is a **left atrial thrombus** (atrial fibrillation) that embolized.
chain: Embolus lodges in a segmental renal artery

idea.rule: Wedge-shaped solid-organ infarcts are usually arterial emboli from the heart.
also: Splenic infarct (cardiac emboli)
Cerebral embolic stroke
Mesenteric embolic ischemia
Limb embolus
